prompt.context: Your client is a seller of car lubricant. It has historically made significant profits, but recently it has come under threat and we have been hired to address three concerns. (1) Over a few previous years consumers believed that they needed to change their oil every 10,000 miles. They have started to realize that in fact they can get away with only changing their oil every 20-30,000 miles. (2) Historically in the US 80% of the market is in DIY (Do It Yourself) and 20% in DIBSE (Do It By Someone Else). This has started to shift in favor of DIBSE. Our client has a 2nd position in the DIY market but only a 10th position in the DIBSE market. (3) The CEO of the lubricant business has promised his shareholders a 200% increase in profits over the next 5 years.
prompt.question: What do you suggest we do?

clarifying_info.q: How is the DIBSE market broken down by outlet type?
clarifying_info.a: 35% of the DIBSE market is Quick Lube, of which 60% is owned by one of our major competitors. 20% is OEM-related dealerships. 15% is small mom-and-pop shops. 10% are small regional chains. 5% are owned by Wal-Mart who are entering this market.

clarifying_info.q: Who is our major DIY customer and what is our position there?
clarifying_info.a: Our major DIY customer is Wal-Mart, where we are the price leader.

clarifying_info.q: How do DIBSE margins compare to DIY margins?
clarifying_info.a: The margins in DIBSE are half the margins in DIY.

clarifying_info.q: What are the fixed costs if the client vertically integrates into DIBSE (opens own garages)?
clarifying_info.a: Marketing $45,000; Rental $36,000; Equipment $15,000; Utilities $14,000; Fixed Labor: 5 mechanics at $40,000 each = $200,000. Total fixed costs = $310,000.

clarifying_info.q: What would the client charge per oil change and what are the variable costs?
clarifying_info.a: The client expects to charge $25 for an oil change and the variable cost per oil change is $20, giving a contribution of $5 per car.
Each garage has three bays. Each oil change takes 15 minutes. Car owners drive their own cars onto the bay. That gives a capacity of 4 cars per bay per hour.

framework: Diagnose the profit decline: reduced oil-change frequency shrinks total market volume; DIY-to-DIBSE shift erodes client share since client is strong in DIY but weak (10th) in DIBSE
Assess DIBSE market entry options: partner/distribute through existing DIBSE channels vs. vertical integration into own garages
Leverage existing Wal-Mart relationship: Wal-Mart is both the dominant DIY customer and a new entrant in DIBSE — explore a supply agreement covering both
Evaluate OEM dealership channel: assess feasibility of brand-linking strategy to drive consumer pull
Consider brand-pull strategy across DIBSE: use strong DIY brand equity to create consumer demand that pulls garages to stock client product
Quantify vertical integration economics: break-even analysis for owning garages; compare to partnership economics
Explore cross-sell / upsell within own garages to improve unit economics if vertical integration is pursued
Formulate recommendation and 200% profit growth roadmap

questions.prompt: Should the client partner with Wal-Mart to access the DIBSE segment? How would you structure such a deal?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify Wal-Mart as the natural first DIBSE partner given the existing DIY relationship. Key rationale: brand trust built in DIY transfers to DIBSE; Wal-Mart is new to DIBSE so a premium lubricant partner adds confidence. Protect DIY margins by negotiating a volume agreement or exclusive supply-location agreement that prevents Wal-Mart from switching DIY suppliers in exchange for DIBSE supply rights.

questions.prompt: Should the client pursue OEM dealership garages? How?
questions.guidance: Direct OEM-level deals are ineffective: in the US each OEM garage independently selects its own lubricants — OEMs have no control over individual dealerships. Instead, create consumer pull via co-advertising at events like the Detroit Auto Show, linking the brand to new premium cars so consumers request the lubricant by name when getting their first oil change. This creates incentive for individual garages to stock the product.

questions.prompt: The client is considering vertically integrating into the DIBSE business by opening its own garages. Does the math support this? (Standard oil change: $25 price, $20 variable cost, 15-minute service, three bays, 10-hour operating day, 300 operating days/year, $310,000 total fixed costs.)
questions.guidance: Walk through the break-even. Identify that capacity is the binding constraint and the model is not viable as-is.

steps: Break-even cars per day = 62,000 / 300 days = ~207 cars/day
Break-even cars per bay per hour = 207 / (3 bays x 10 hours) = ~6.9 cars/bay/hour
Actual capacity = 60 min / 15 min per car = 4 cars/bay/hour
6.9 > 4: required throughput exceeds physical capacity — model does not work
math.answer: The garage requires ~6.9 cars/bay/hour to break even but can only handle 4 cars/bay/hour. Vertical integration as a pure oil-change business is not viable.

questions.prompt: If the garage cross-sells other products, the price rises to $48 and variable costs rise to $28, but each service now takes 45 minutes. Does this revised model work?
questions.guidance: Recalculate contribution and required throughput; compare to new capacity. Conclusion: still not viable, but the gap has narrowed significantly.

math.setup: New variable contribution = $48 - $28 = $20 per car. Fixed costs remain $310,000.
steps: Break-even cars per bay per hour = 52 / (3 x 10) = ~1.7 cars/bay/hour
1.7 > 1.3: still cannot break even, though much closer than before
math.answer: Cross-selling raises unit contribution fourfold (from $5 to $20) and cuts required throughput to ~1.7 cars/bay/hour, but physical capacity is only ~1.3 cars/bay/hour. The model is still not viable under current assumptions.

questions.prompt: The CEO stops you in the elevator and asks for a quick update. What do you say?
questions.guidance: Candidate should give a crisp, structured 30-second summary: root cause, what has been evaluated, what is recommended, and next steps.

brainstorming.prompt: What additional strategies could the client use to grow its presence in the DIBSE segment and achieve the 200% profit growth target?

categories.name: Channel partnerships
ideas: Supply deal with Wal-Mart DIBSE garages leveraging existing DIY relationship
Negotiate preferred-supplier agreements with regional chains (10% of DIBSE)
Target mom-and-pop shops (15% of DIBSE) with attractive margin incentives

categories.name: Brand and marketing
ideas: Co-advertise at automotive events (e.g., Detroit Auto Show) to create consumer pull
Link brand to premium/new-car launches to drive consumer requests at garages
Loyalty or warranty programs that specify client lubricant

categories.name: Product and pricing
ideas: Develop DIBSE-specific SKUs or formulations to justify premium pricing
Bundle lubricant with other car care products for garages
Introduce a premium product line targeting high-end car owners in DIBSE

categories.name: Vertical integration (own garages)
ideas: Cross-sell wiper blades, air filters, car wash while customer waits to improve unit economics
Acquire or franchise existing Quick Lube outlets not controlled by competitor
Pilot a small number of garages to test economics before scaling

categories.name: Volume recovery
ideas: Educate consumers on benefits of more-frequent changes (engine longevity, warranty)
Offer seasonal promotions to increase change frequency
Target fleet operators (taxis, delivery companies) who change oil more frequently

recommendation: The primary near-term action is to negotiate a supply agreement with Wal-Mart covering its new DIBSE garages, protecting the DIY relationship while gaining DIBSE distribution
Use strong DIY brand equity to create consumer pull across all DIBSE channels through targeted advertising and co-branding at automotive events
Do not vertically integrate into garages at this time — neither pure oil-change nor cross-sell service models break even under current capacity constraints
risks: If Wal-Mart gains leverage in DIBSE it may renegotiate DIY terms unfavorably
DIBSE margins are half of DIY, so volume gains may not fully offset profit pressure from the frequency shift
Competitors who control Quick Lube (60% of 35% of DIBSE) are entrenched and may respond aggressively
next_steps: Conduct detailed analysis of Wal-Mart DIBSE supply deal terms and margin impact over 5 years
Model consumer pull impact of Detroit Auto Show and similar co-advertising investments
Explore whether cross-sell economics can be improved further (faster service tech, higher-margin add-ons) to make a garage pilot viable
